executive_summary: AUD/CAD trades at 0.99321 (gated price store close, spotDate 2026-09-03), meaning one Australian dollar buys 0.99321 Canadian dollars, and it sits 68 pips below parity at the 96th percentile of its 52-week closing range after gaining 0.44% over one month, 1.03% over three months, 2.18% over six months and 8.20% over twelve. The dominant bilateral narrative is the widest interest-rate differential this cross has offered in years — 210bp, with the RBA at 4.35% against a Bank of Canada that held for a seventh consecutive decision on 2026-09-02 — set against the most severe divergence in external accounts between the two economies in two decades. Three bilateral differentials matter more than anything either standalone dossier emphasises: a core inflation gap of roughly 165bp (Australian trimmed mean 3.6% against Canadian CPI-trim 1.9% and CPI-median 2.0%) that gives only one of the two central banks a live reason to act; a relative BIS real effective exchange rate gap of roughly 21% with AUD expensive at 115.92 and CAD nearly the cheapest currency in the G10 at 95.71; and a terms-of-trade configuration in which Australia's dominant export sits at the floor of its annual range while Canada's is elevated, tariff-exempt and supported into 2027. Positioning is the amplified maximum the framework recognises — leveraged funds long 54,061 AUD contracts and short 72,092 CAD contracts, with dealers holding the mirror on both legs — so the pair trade is the consensus trade rather than a by-product of two independent views. The settled direction verdict is Bullish on both horizons, conviction 3 tactically at a net score of +0.2143 and conviction 2 strategically at +0.1152, and the report is written around it. Where this analysis parts company with the verdict is not on direction but on entry: the pair is being bought at the 96th percentile of its range, above every two-touch price cluster in 4,879 weekday bars of stored history, with no qualifying resistance zone anywhere overhead and the nearest four-touch support 632 pips (6.36%) below — a configuration in which 210bp of carry is the only thing actually paying you, and the forward curve at −231.1bp annualised has already taken more than that back.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no quoted purchasing-power-parity series for this cross, so the valuation read is built from the relative BIS real effective exchange rates carried in both dossiers, on June 2026 observations that sit roughly 63 days before the valuation date and marginally outside the 60-day strategic freshness window. Australia's REER of 115.92 is the highest in the eleven-currency benchmark set and follows a +10.36-point twelve-month real appreciation, more than double the next-largest move; Canada's REER of 95.71 is the second cheapest after the yen and is down 3.41 points over the same year. That is a relative real gap of 21.1% with AUD expensive, and it is the single largest valuation dislocation available anywhere in the AUD complex. Mechanically closing the whole gap would imply a level near 0.82, which is not a forecast; a reversion of one quarter of it over the strategic horizon implies roughly 0.943, still 5% below spot. What is priced at 0.99321 is a market that has fully absorbed the 210bp differential, the Canadian tariff rupture and the Australian rate repricing, and has priced none of the real exchange rate gap or the two-decade-wide divergence in current accounts. This valuation signal has essentially no tactical actionability but strategically it is the principal reason the direction verdict clears the Bullish threshold by only 0.0152.

On spot 0.99321 that differential is worth approximately 209 pips per year, roughly 17.4 pips per month. The carry-to-vol ratio is 0.318 on the estimated 94.7-day ATM implied volatility of 6.611%, an upper bound because the vol denominator is a documented low-biased estimate; on realised-vol bases the ratio is 0.376–0.409. Carry regime is working, but not as generously as the differential implies, because the forward curve has already taken more than the carry back: the CME calendar-spread funding premium is −231.1bp annualised, exceeding the +210bp policy differential by roughly 21bp of embedded cross-currency basis working against a long AUD/CAD carry position. The practical implication is that this is a carry trade only against spot; against the market's own pricing (the forward) it is a directional bet that the pair does not fall by more than the forward already assumes.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +210bp in AUD's favour: the RBA cash rate target is 4.35% against a Bank of Canada overnight target of 2.25%, confirmed held again on 2026-09-02 for a seventh consecutive decision. The bilateral 10-year differential is +141.1bp, but both legs are the monthly series as of 2026-06-01 and cannot be quoted as live levels. The tactical case rests on sequencing rather than level, and the sequencing is one-sided: the gated calendar puts the RBA on 2026-09-29 and gives Canada no scheduled decision until 2026-10-28, so inside a four-week window only one of the two banks can move, and the only move it is plausibly going to make is a hike. Roughly 47-50% is priced for an RBA move to 4.60% with about 30bp of cumulative tightening priced by February 2027; the base dossier's own view is that September is nearer 35% than 50%, which is a mild offset, but a partial unwind of RBA pricing still leaves the differential unchanged rather than compressed. Transmission is direct and mechanical: AUD/CAD is a pure interest-differential cross with almost no bilateral trade to complicate it, so front-end repricing passes through to spot with little friction. The counterweight is that forwards already discount the entire carry and then some.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the +210bp differential is the most durable fundamental support this pair has, and it is unusually well protected on both sides. The RBA's own published forecasts do not return underlying inflation to the 2-3% midpoint until early 2028, so an easing cycle inside the horizon is close to unavailable; the Bank of Canada, meanwhile, is at 2.25% with core measures sitting exactly at target on the trim-median average and has now held seven times running. The compression risk is real but bounded. Canadian OIS carries roughly 65% of a 2026 hike, two of the six largest Canadian banks forecast 2.75% by December, and one house cited after the September decision projects 75bp of hikes beginning in the fourth quarter; against that, CIBC's chief economist saw little prospect of a change in either direction in 2026 and the Bank's own market-participants survey median reaches 2.50% only in March 2027. Even the most hawkish Canadian path of 75bp, with the RBA adding 25bp, leaves the differential at roughly 160bp — still the widest AUD spread outside CHF, JPY, SEK and EUR. The dated tests are the RBA on 2026-11-03 and 2026-12-08 and the Bank of Canada on 2026-10-28 with its Monetary Policy Report and 2026-12-09; the 28 October projection round is where Canadian hike pricing is most likely to be validated or removed. Confidence falls from tactical because a six-month window contains two Canadian decisions rather than none, and because the forward curve already charges more than the carry.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is the decisive bilateral fact and it runs strongly in AUD's favour on the measure that drives policy. Australia's RBA trimmed mean is 3.6% year on year and has been flat at that level for four consecutive months, with headline at 3.5% in the July monthly indicator against a 3.2% consensus and services inflation rising from 3.5% to 3.7%. Canada's preferred core measures are CPI-trim at 1.9% and CPI-median at 2.0%, averaging exactly to target, with headline at 3.0% only because gasoline is up 25.7% year on year. That is a core inflation gap of roughly 160-170bp, and it is the reason the RBA has an active hiking debate while the Bank of Canada does not. Growth cuts the other way in the most recent quarter but not decisively: Canada printed 3.3% annualised in Q2 against the Bank's own 2.5% call while Australia printed 0.4% quarter on quarter, above the 0.3% consensus but decelerating to 2.1% year on year from 2.5%. Both economies therefore delivered upside GDP surprises inside the same 48 hours, which largely cancels; on annual growth Australia is still ahead at 2.1% against Canada's 0.99%. Labour markets invert the reading: Australian unemployment at 4.5% is a post-COVID high and rising, Canadian unemployment at 6.4% is a two-year low and falling for a third month, so levels favour Australia and momentum favours Canada. Transmission is asymmetric: Australian CPI is quarterly with a monthly indicator and moves the pair far harder than Canadian CPI, because the Australian print is the one attached to a live hike.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both economies are decelerating and the differential stops being informative, which makes Neutral the honest answer rather than a default. On the Australian side the growth deterioration is broad and measurable: unemployment at a post-COVID high of 4.5%, private new capital expenditure down 3.6% quarter on quarter against a +0.8% consensus, construction work done down 2.1%, NAB business confidence at −19 and twenty-two points below its long-run average, and six-month annualised growth running near 1.5% against 2.8% in the second half of 2025. Australian inflation also grinds down on the RBA's own path to 3.3% by end-2026, which removes the acceleration that is currently driving the currency without removing the level that justifies the rate. On the Canadian side the picture is the mirror image at a different point in the cycle: Q2 was the strongest quarter in three years but the July advance estimate was flat at 0.0% and was measured before the 50% Section 338 duties took effect and before Canadian counter-measures on 2026-09-08, so Q3 and Q4 carry a mechanical tariff drag against a household sector with debt at 179.6% of disposable income. Canadian core is already at target and headline should converge down as the gasoline base effect rolls off, while Australian core stays above target through 2027. The net is a widening inflation gap in AUD's favour set against a growth deterioration that is arguably further advanced in Australia than in Canada, where the shock is dated but has not yet landed. Those forces are close to balanced and neither is forecastable at six months with useful skill.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD/CAD belongs in the framework's low-risk-sensitivity bucket, and the reason is that both currencies are long global growth. AUD is the textbook high-beta risk proxy and the most liquid G10 expression of China sentiment; CAD carries a mild positive risk beta with a documented USD/CAD-to-equities correlation of -0.2 to -0.3, roughly half the Antipodean sensitivity. The pair therefore has a modest positive risk beta equal to the difference, so a benign regime helps AUD/CAD a little and a violent risk-off hurts it a lot more than either leg's standalone beta suggests. The current regime is unambiguously benign: VIX at 14.51 and down 3.70 points on the month, US investment grade OAS at 79bp, high yield OAS at 263bp having tightened 21bp, and the S&P 500 roughly 16% higher year to date. That marginally favours the higher-beta leg. What cancels it is the demand-anchor differential. Australia's dominant external customer is China, which takes roughly 30-35% of its exports and whose manufacturing PMI is 49.8 and still in contraction, with the Bank of Canada's own September statement noting that China's economy slowed while United States growth remained solid on consumer spending and AI investment. Canada's demand anchor is therefore the stronger economy — except that the tariff regime is actively severing Canada's access to it, which is the one thing that stops this observation from being decisively bearish for the pair. Benign risk plus a weakening Chinese anchor plus a severed American one nets to no signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At one to six months the risk regime is not forecastable with useful skill, and for this pair specifically it is close to irrelevant because the residual beta is small. What can be assessed is the shape of the distribution and its bilateral asymmetry. VIX at 14.51 and high yield OAS at 263bp sit near the tight end of their post-2020 ranges, so the strategic distribution is skewed toward widening rather than tightening; in that widening, AUD's documented risk-off convexity is more violent than CAD's, which makes the pair's tail left-skewed even though its modal beta is near zero. Two structural flows partly offset that. Australian superannuation funds running roughly A$4.3trn generate mechanical AUD buying while global equities rise and selling when they fall, which amplifies the same convexity. Canadian pension funds (CPPIB, OTPP and peers) run the mirror hedging programme on their own foreign assets, generating mechanical CAD demand when foreign asset values rise. Because both systems hedge in the same direction against the same global equity beta, the two flows partly neutralise each other within this cross, which is a genuinely pair-specific observation and not derivable from either dossier alone. Add that oil strength is currently supply-driven rather than demand-driven, which severs the usual link between the risk regime and CAD's terms of trade, and the honest strategic conclusion is that this factor delivers no direction and only a modest left tail.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the amplified configuration the framework warns about, and it is the clearest bearish input on the tactical horizon. On the CFTC report covering 2026-08-25, leveraged funds were net long 54,061 AUD contracts, 18.2% of open interest on the cached basis and the highest reading in the cached series, while leveraged funds were net short 72,092 CAD contracts with asset managers short a further 58,943 for a combined Canadian speculative short of 131,035. Specs are therefore long the base leg and short the quote leg simultaneously, which means the implied AUD/CAD position is not merely crowded but maximally crowded: the pair trade itself is the consensus trade, not a by-product of two independent views. The marginal flow is the tactical signal and it points the other way from the stock. Canadian shorts covered 65,515 contracts in the fortnight to 2026-08-25, a 33% reduction, with open interest falling 8.4% — that is position liquidation, and covering a CAD short means buying CAD, which pushes AUD/CAD down. Australian leveraged longs meanwhile added a further 5,520 contracts. So the pair is being bought by the slower money and sold by the faster money at exactly the point where the implied position is most extended. Dealers are the mirror on both legs: short 33,186 AUD contracts and long 124,930 CAD contracts, meaning the street's inventory on both sides of this cross is positioned for the pair to fall and it will not add to a further rally. Australian options corroborate from a different angle, with 25-delta risk reversals negative at every tenor and deepening with maturity.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning has almost no forecasting power at one to six months on either leg, because both books turn over inside the horizon. The Australian leveraged net travelled from +29,683 to +24,788 to +48,541 in five weeks, and the Canadian combined speculative short moved 65,515 contracts in a fortnight; whatever is on either book today will not be on it in February. What survives is the structural layer, and for this cross it is genuinely two-sided. Australian asset managers have held a persistent net short between -31,709 and -45,427 contracts in every cached week, reflecting AUD's role as a funding currency, while Canadian asset managers have halved their short from -108,343 to -58,943 — real money is capitulating on the bearish CAD trade at the same time as it stays structurally short AUD, which is a bilateral flow pointing against the pair. Offsetting that, Canada absorbed a record C$80.8bn of foreign purchases of government bonds in Q2, an allocation decision rather than a speculative position, arriving in the same quarter the current account swung to surplus — Canada is funding itself without needing a weaker currency, which removes one classic mechanism by which AUD/CAD would rise. On the other side, Japanese retail and institutional demand for Australian dollar assets strengthens with the AUD-JPY spread and has no Canadian analogue of similar size. Structural real-money shorts on both legs, offsetting pension hedging programmes and a record Canadian bond inflow net to approximately flat.

If the RBA holds on 2026-09-29 while Canadian covering continues, the pair faces simultaneous selling from both legs of its own consensus, and there is no third participant identified to absorb it.

Whichever capitulates first sets the pair's direction, and there is no reliable way to rank them ex ante.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Commodity-versus-commodity pair: AUD/CAD is structurally an iron-ore-against-oil trade, and the framework identifies exactly this configuration as grounds for boosting Factor 5. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Start with what does not matter: direct bilateral trade is immaterial. On IMF DOTS 2024 data, Australia exported US$2.1bn of goods to Canada and imported US$2.7bn, for a net Australian deficit of US$0.6bn — a rounding error against either country's total trade, and it means there is no bilateral trade-flow channel to speak of in this cross. What matters instead is that the two economies sell competing commodity bundles into the same world, and right now those bundles are moving in opposite directions. Canada's is priced off oil: Brent was US$90.135 and WTI US$85.446 on 2026-08-31, both up more than 2.3% on the day, the diesel crack exceeded US$100/bbl for the first time, and critically energy, potash, fish and critical minerals were all carved out of the 50% Section 338 tariff regime, so Canada's largest export category trades on world prices rather than bilateral politics. Australia's is priced off iron ore, roughly 35% of export revenue, sitting at US$95.34/t essentially at the floor of a US$93.66-111.42 annual range. The external accounts have already registered the difference in the most direct way available: Canada posted a Q2 current account surplus of C$8.8bn, the first since 2022 and the largest since 2005, while Australia posted a record A$27.1bn deficit in Q1 with a A$-29.7bn consensus for Q2 and a current account at -3.68% of GDP. Australia's offsets are real — Newcastle coal near US$130/t and Japanese LNG at US$19.0/mmbtu roughly 75% above pre-conflict levels — but the June-quarter national accounts recorded Australian terms of trade falling again, so the offset is not winning.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At the applied 0.18 weight this is the largest bearish contribution in the strategic score, and three separate strands point the same way. First, the external balance differential is extreme and moving further apart: Canada's Q2 surplus of C$8.8bn is the largest in twenty-one years and was achieved on goods trade rather than one-off income items, financed by a record C$80.8bn of foreign sovereign bond purchases, while Australia's record deficit is driven by the income balance and the imported energy bill and is forecast to widen again. Second, the terms-of-trade paths diverge structurally rather than cyclically. Australia's energy windfall is explicitly temporary — Westpac forecasts Newcastle coal easing from US$130/t toward US$120/t and Japanese LNG peaking at US$18.5/mmbtu this quarter — while iron ore faces roughly 20Mt of new Simandou supply into a Chinese steel demand base that ING expects to stagnate long term. Canada's oil support is the opposite: the EIA sees roughly 0.6mb/d of Strait of Hormuz disruption persisting to end-2027 and Brent averaging US$87/bbl for 2026, a multi-quarter supply-side revenue transfer to non-Gulf producers, capped only by a WCS-WTI differential near US$12/bbl. Third, and most starkly, the relative real exchange rate. Australia's BIS REER is 115.92 for June 2026, the highest in the eleven-currency set after a +10.36-point twelve-month real appreciation; Canada's is 95.71, the second cheapest after the yen and down 3.41 points over the same year. That is a relative real gap of roughly 21% with AUD expensive, into the worse of the two external positions. Overvaluation plus a record deficit against cheapness plus a record surplus is the textbook mean-reversion configuration.

net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the framework's direction rules leg by leg. Oil up: ++CAD against +AUD (mild), so the quote leg gains more than the base leg and the pair FALLS — oil strength is bearish AUD/CAD. Iron ore up: ++AUD against a negligible Canadian effect, so the pair RISES — iron ore is the only clean bullish commodity lever in this cross. LNG and thermal coal up: strongly ++AUD, mildly +CAD through gas, so the pair rises, but both are forecast to peak this quarter. Netting the current configuration: oil is at US$90 and supported into 2027 by a supply disruption the EIA expects to persist, while iron ore sits at the floor of its annual range with new supply arriving and consensus averages below spot. The single largest Australian lever is pinned at its low and the single largest Canadian lever is elevated and structurally supported. Net effect: clearly bearish AUD/CAD, and more so strategically than tactically because the Australian coal and LNG offset is explicitly forecast to fade while the Canadian oil support is not.

CAD gains strongly on export receipts and terms of trade, with the energy complex tariff-exempt so the gain is unimpaired; AUD gains mildly and gets a partly offsetting hit through a higher imported energy bill that is already driving its record current account deficit. net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: The iron-ore-to-Brent ratio. Neither commodity alone determines this cross; what determines it is the relative price of Australia's dominant export against Canada's, and that ratio is currently near the weak end of its recent history with iron ore at US$95.34/t against Brent at US$90.135/bbl — a ratio of 1.06. Watching either in isolation will mislead. Independent commentary makes the same structural point: AUD/CAD's commodity divergence works in the pair's favour when iron ore and oil move in opposite directions, but when a global demand shock hits both commodities at once the divergence collapses and the pair flattens into a narrow range or whipsaws.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two central banks are communicating in materially different registers, and the divergence favours the base leg. The RBA held unanimously on 11 August with an explicit conditional hiking sentence, and its 25 August minutes disclosed that the Board actively debated a pre-emptive 25bp increase and named the monthly inflation, employment and housing reports as the evidence that would settle the question before its next meeting — a central bank publishing its own reaction function and then receiving data that satisfies it, which is why five sell-side houses changed published forecasts inside seventy-two hours. The Bank of Canada, by contrast, held for a seventh consecutive decision on 2026-09-02 and delivered a deliberately two-sided message: it said that the upside risks to inflation have increased, while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain, and commentary on the day characterised the Bank as being in wait-and-see mode with the uncertain outlook preventing clear signals for the rest of the year. That is not a dovish message — it is a marginal hawkish shift on inflation risk, and it is the single most important update to the quote dossier's own view, which had expected Canadian hike pricing to bleed out. But a bank that refuses to signal is not a bank that will move, and CIBC's chief economist saw little prospect of a change in either direction in 2026. Sequencing reinforces: the RBA decides on 2026-09-29 with no Canadian meeting until 2026-10-28, so the base leg sets the tone unopposed inside the window.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the credibility differential matters more than the tone differential, and both banks are highly credible, which means the question is which one's published reaction function anchors the differential better. The RBA's does: it has published forecasts showing inflation above the 2-3% midpoint until early 2028 and has stated it will do what is necessary including raising the cash rate further if upside risks materialise, and a central bank with that forecast and that framing does not begin easing inside six months. That anchors the front end of the Australian curve and, by extension, the carry that is this pair's principal support. The Bank of Canada's reaction function is more conditional in both directions: it has committed publicly not to let higher oil prices become persistent inflation while simultaneously agreeing to look through the direct effects of oil, and its July deliberations disclosed a range of views among Governing Council members about the sustainability of the rebound. The decisive dated event is 2026-10-28, when the Bank publishes a Monetary Policy Report — a projection round, which moves a pair materially harder than a bare statement. There it must simultaneously mark growth for tariff drag and mark inflation for a gasoline base effect that is rolling off, and that combination is more likely to remove Canadian hike pricing than to validate it. The offsets that keep confidence at 55 rather than higher are that the September statement leaned hawkish on inflation risk, that two large Canadian banks forecast 2.75% by December, and that the RBA's own hawkishness is conditional on an oil shock it does not control.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Asymmetric bilateral event risk concentrated entirely on the quote leg: a permanent, dated and escalating tariff regime against a base currency with no comparable political exposure. This is the one factor where the two legs are not comparable in kind. Raised +0.01 on both horizons.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk in this cross is not balanced, it is loaded onto Canada. The United States imposed 50% Section 338 duties on roughly US$20bn of Canadian goods across 554 tariff lines on 2026-08-22 — the first presidential use of that authority since 1949, applied regardless of USMCA preference and carrying no expiry date — and talks collapsed with no new negotiations planned. Canada's own retaliation on roughly US$20bn of American goods at 15-50% takes effect on 2026-09-08, inside the tactical window, and the product-level composition was not published as of the valuation date, so the market cannot have priced it; Ottawa's counter-measures are also self-inflicted cost on a domestic price level. Against that, Australia carries essentially no bilateral political risk: its next federal election is not due until May 2028 and it has no analogous trade rupture. The two shared exposures partly offset. The Middle East conflict is genuinely two-sided for both legs — it lifts Australian coal and LNG and Canadian oil while damaging global growth and keeping both central banks hawkish — but the commodity netting in Factor 5 means it favours the quote leg on balance. China is the base-leg-specific tail, with manufacturing PMI at 49.8 and the Bank of Canada itself noting that China slowed while United States growth stayed solid. Net across the window: the dated, unpriced binary is Canadian and it is negative for the quote leg, which is bullish for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At one to six months the Canadian exposure stops being a series of dates and becomes a structural condition, which is what makes this factor stronger strategically than tactically. Section 338 permits proclamation-only tariffs with no investigation and no time limit, so there is no statutory clock forcing the parties back to the table; the escalation path is already announced, with duties on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel rising to 50% from 2027-01-01; and the USMCA architecture that would normally constrain this was destabilised when the six-year review was triggered on 2026-07-01 with United States-Mexico talks proceeding on a separate track and Canada absent. Ottawa's own planning assumption is that no substantive talks resume before the 2026-11-03 midterms, and support measures are being designed to outlast the current American administration. The magnitude is bounded — US$20bn is roughly 5.2% of the US$382bn Canada shipped south in 2025, with energy carved out — but the duration is not, and the Bank of Canada's September statement explicitly acknowledged that both the conflict and the trade situation remain fluid, with further tariffs capable of jeopardising the recovery. Australia's strategic event set contains nothing of comparable specificity: its exposures are the oil shock, which it sits on both sides of, and Chinese demand, which is a slow bleed rather than a dated event. The one dated risk that could reverse this factor is the midterms producing a negotiation restart, which the quote dossier assigns roughly 25%.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs are top-tier sovereigns and neither has a dated fiscal event inside the tactical window, so this factor carries no tradeable bilateral signal over four weeks and Neutral is the considered rather than default answer. Australia is AAA at S&P — affirmed with a stable outlook in August 2026 — AAA at Fitch and Aaa at Moody's, with federal net debt reported near 19.9% of GDP and an underlying cash deficit of 1.0% of GDP. Canada is AAA at S&P, Aaa at Moody's and AAA at DBRS but AA+ at Fitch, with federal debt-to-GDP projected above 43% by 2027-28 and a 2025-26 deficit revised down to C$66.9bn. On the numbers Australia is the stronger sovereign by a wide margin; on the market's treatment of them the difference is invisible, because both fund themselves without difficulty and Canada absorbed a record C$80.8bn of foreign government bond purchases in Q2. The next Australian fiscal event is MYEFO in December and the next budget in May 2027; Canada's Spring Economic Update was tabled on 2026-04-28. The one live consideration is that Canada's tariff support package is explicitly open-ended and unbudgeted, so a costing announced around the 2026-09-08 retaliation date would be a new datapoint — but even a large package does not move a AAA sovereign inside four weeks. Transmission to this cross is therefore negligible at this horizon.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal differential becomes a modest, low-volatility bullish input for the pair. Australia carries net debt near 20% of GDP with an underlying deficit of 1.0% of GDP and a AAA rating from all three major agencies with a stable outlook; Canada carries federal debt above 43% of GDP by 2027-28, a deficit near 2% of GDP, a Fitch rating one notch below Australia's, and — uniquely — an explicitly open-ended and unbudgeted tariff support commitment that Ottawa is designing to outlast the current American administration, set against a shrinking tariff-exposed tax base. Australia also offers the higher yield on the better balance sheet: its ten-year sits above Canada's by 141.1bp on the monthly June series, which is the highest AAA-rated developed-market yield available against a sovereign carrying roughly half Canada's debt ratio. The qualifications are real and cap confidence at 52. Australia's own trajectory is one-directional, with net debt projected to rise toward 21.9% by 2029-30 and no return to balance until the mid-2030s, and Australian state government debt is rising faster than federal. Canada retains the lowest net debt-to-GDP in the G7 and its long end is orderly, with the thirty-year at 4.15%, so no fiscal risk premium is being applied. Neither sovereign is a source of downside for its currency inside the horizon; the differential is a relative-quality tilt rather than a driver, and it is scored accordingly at a 0.07 weight.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor where the pair's own market data is the legitimate subject, and this pass is deliberately given very little of it — no moving averages, no zones, no trailing returns, no ATR. What is supplied is the volatility surface and one structural note, and both counsel Neutral. The estimated at-the-money implied vol term structure is 6.264% at 38.6 days, 6.611% at 94.7 days and 6.937% at 185.7 days: contango, with no backwardation kink despite an RBA decision on 2026-09-29 falling inside the front tenor and a Bank of Canada projection round on 2026-10-28 inside the second. risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The spot distribution is negatively skewed — the 25% downside case is 1.20 times the size of the equally probable upside case — and every unit of positive expected value comes from the carry rather than from the price, which is a defensible position and a small one. Position sizing note: the strategic stop belongs on a weekly close below 0.9640 (292 pips, 6.2 ATR, −2.94% from spot, below the 200-day and the upper reach of the 0.96803–0.97736 two-touch band), implying roughly 0.34x notional per 1% account-risk unit — about a third of the tactical size, reflecting the wider invalidation distance to the nearest well-tested support.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish, conviction 3, base case AUD/CAD 0.9990 (+58 pips) inside two to four weeks
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bullish, conviction 2, base case AUD/CAD 1.0020 (+88 pips), probability-weighted expected spot 0.99600 over one to six months
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: +432 pips (4.5%) above the Exchange Rates UK aggregate's December 2026 figure of 0.95280; approximately +210 pips above the derived named-bank cross centre of roughly 0.975
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three weightings explain the divergence. First, we weight the meeting calendar rather than the annual forecast — inside the tactical window only the RBA meets, and a differential that cannot compress before the window closes is worth more than a six-month point estimate. Second, we weight the guidance wedge on the quote leg, where roughly 65% of a 2026 Canadian hike is priced against a Bank survey median reaching 2.50% only in March 2027, with the 2026-10-28 projection round the dated test. Third, we treat the Canadian tariff regime as a structural condition with no expiry and a dated 2027-01-01 escalation rather than as a negotiation that resolves, which the aggregates implicitly assume. Where we agree with the bears is Factor 5, scored at our highest strategic confidence of 70: a 21% relative real exchange rate gap into the widest current account divergence in two decades is a real objection, and it is why the strategic score clears the threshold by only 0.0152. It is also worth recording a credibility check: National Australia Bank was reported as seeing the pair rising to only 0.94 by mid-2026, a level the pair had already exceeded by roughly 5.6% at the valuation date, suggesting pair-level forecasts for this cross have systematically underestimated the carry.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The differential accrues while the pair does not fall — 210bp of carry against a forward that discounts 231bp, so approximately +143 pips of forward-relative expected value over six months, concentrated in the tactical window where the calendar is one-sided. Being right about the 2026-10-28 Monetary Policy Report is the specific event that converts the tactical view into a strategic one.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The bears are right for the reason we half-concede. Iron ore breaking its annual low while Brent holds above US$90 would push Factor 5 to maximum confidence, and with the implied pair position at its amplified maximum and dealers mirrored on both legs, an unwind would be reinforced by both legs of its own consensus simultaneously — the −382 pip downside case, and possibly worse given there is no well-tested support until 6.36% lower.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The stances agree but the composition and the conviction do not, and the difference is almost entirely two factors being reweighted. Factor 2 carries 0.18 tactically and 0.10 strategically and its stance also moves from Bullish to Neutral, removing 0.1044 from the score; Factor 5 carries 0.08 tactically and 0.18 strategically and its confidence rises from 60 to 70, taking its contribution from −0.0480 to −0.1260. Those two changes account for essentially the whole 0.0991 gap between the scores. The economic content is that over two to four weeks the pair trades the relative reaction function, where a 165bp core inflation gap and a one-sided meeting calendar favour the base leg, while over one to six months it trades the balance of payments and the real exchange rate, where a roughly 21% relative REER gap and the widest current account divergence in twenty years favour the quote leg. Factor 1's own confidence also falls from 66 to 58, because the differential is unmovable inside four weeks and merely wide over six months.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 2026-10-28 Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report — the only projection round on either leg inside either horizon — followed six days later by the RBA decision on 2026-11-03. That fortnight is where Canadian hike pricing is validated or removed and where the RBA either delivers or defers, and it is the handover point between the tactical and strategic readings.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The two horizons say the same thing with different confidence, so there is no divergence to navigate — there is a decay to respect. The tactical Bullish rests on a calendar that expires on 2026-09-29; the strategic Bullish rests on carry alone and is 0.0152 from Neutral. Practically, that means the case for the pair is strongest between now and the RBA decision, weakest across the 2026-10-28 projection round, and requires Factor 5 to be re-underwritten — specifically iron ore against Brent, and the Australian Q3 current account — before any strategic exposure is treated as independent of the tactical one. In price terms: carry the tactical position with the 0.9840 stop into 2026-09-29, and do not roll it into the strategic window at more than the 0.34x notional the wider 0.9640 stop implies without re-testing the commodity ratio.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey (August) and Ivey PMI; CFTC Commitments of Traders release
catalysts.rationale: Canadian employment consensus is roughly +15.8k after July's +75.1k with unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%, so the bar is lowered and a beat would firm the quote leg. The same day's positioning data shows whether the 65,515-contract Canadian short covering continued, which mechanically buys CAD and pushes the pair down irrespective of any Canadian fundamental improvement.

catalysts.event: Canadian retaliatory tariffs take effect on roughly US$20bn of United States goods at 15-50%
catalysts.rationale: The date and headline amount are known but the product-level composition was unpublished at the valuation date, so the market cannot have priced the sector mix or the probability of further American escalation in response. Because Canada's economy is roughly a tenth the size of its counterpart, dollar-for-dollar retaliation is proportionally heavier on the quote leg, and it raises Canadian domestic prices while reducing choice — a growth-negative, inflation-positive shock with no base-leg analogue.

The most important quote-leg data point in the tactical window. CPI-trim at 1.9% and CPI-median at 2.0% average exactly to target, with the entire 100bp headline-core gap attributable to gasoline up 25.7% year on year. If trim rises toward 2.2% the oil-broadening risk the Bank of Canada said it would respond to becomes live and the 210bp differential starts to look compressible, which is bearish for the pair; if trim slips, the statistical basis for a Canadian hike disappears and the pair's carry support strengthens.

catalysts.event: Federal Open Market Committee decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A third-currency event dated from both dossiers rather than the gated AUD/CAD calendar. Roughly 58-60% is priced for a 25bp hike after Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote, with the path to about 3.90% by November. A hawkish outcome places the dollar at the United States-exceptionalism end of the smile, where both pro-cyclical legs lose but the base leg historically loses more, so the net for the pair is negative. A hold would be the larger surprise and would favour the higher-beta base leg.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board decision
catalysts.rationale: The single largest binary in the tactical window and the only scheduled decision on either leg inside it, per the gated calendar with no projection round attached. Roughly 47-50% is priced for a hike to 4.60%, which would take the bilateral differential from 210bp to 235bp with no Canadian meeting until 28 October to offset it. The statement language matters as much as the decision: removal of the conditional hiking sentence would be a dovish surprise into a market positioned the other way on both legs of this cross.

The first Canadian print in which the gasoline base effect turns materially less favourable and the first that can capture two-way tariff pass-through — American duties raising Canadian export costs and Canadian counter-duties raising import prices. Headline converging down toward core at 2.0% removes the statistical support for the roughly 65% of Canadian 2026 hike pricing, which protects the pair's 210bp differential and lands eight days before the Bank's projection round.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The identified inflection point between the two horizons and the most consequential dated event in this cross — the only projection round on either leg in either horizon per the gated calendar. The Bank must publish a full forecast round that simultaneously marks growth for tariff drag and marks inflation for a gasoline base effect rolling off, and it must do so against market pricing of roughly 65% for a 2026 hike and its own survey median of 2.50% only in March 2027. Removal of that hike pricing widens the effective differential and is bullish for the pair; delivery of a hike to 2.50% compresses it to 185bp and is the cleanest single invalidation of the carry thesis.

catalysts.event: Australia Q3 Consumer Price Index (quarterly ABS release, final week of October)
catalysts.rationale: Australia publishes headline and trimmed mean quarterly, which compresses three months of expectations into one number and produces outsized base-leg reactions. This print resolves the central market disagreement — whether the July acceleration to a 3.6% trimmed mean was signal, as NAB, CBA, ANZ and Goldman argue, or noise, as Westpac maintains — and therefore whether the 165bp core inflation gap that underpins Factor 2 survives into the strategic horizon. Date approximate to the release week rather than confirmed to the day.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia decision with the quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy
catalysts.rationale: CBA, ANZ, Goldman Sachs and UBS all locate the RBA hike to 4.60% here rather than in September, and the accompanying Statement on Monetary Policy is the base leg's highest-signal communication in the strategic window because the RBA signals its path through forecast revisions rather than explicit guidance. An upward revision opens a path toward 4.85% and widens the differential further; a downward revision closes the cycle and removes the pair's principal support six days after the Canadian projection round.

The only dated circuit-breaker for the tariff regime inside the strategic horizon, and the sole mechanism that would reverse Factor 7. Ottawa's own planning assumption is that no substantive talks resume before this date; American consumers absorbed more than US$231bn in tariff costs between February 2025 and January 2026, so the transmission channel is domestic political pressure rather than negotiation. A credible restart reprices the quote leg's entire risk premium in one move because Section 338 duties are removable by proclamation with no statutory process.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia decision followed by the Bank of Canada decision (2026-12-09)
catalysts.rationale: Consecutive decisions on both legs of the cross in a single 24-hour window, the only such clustering in the horizon and an event that amplifies rather than cancels because the pair reprices twice in the same direction if both surprise. An Australian hike to 4.60% is close to fully priced by December, so delivery is neutral and non-delivery is sharply negative for the pair; the Canadian decision carries the residual of roughly 65% of 2026 hike pricing, so a hike compresses the differential to 185bp the following morning.

catalysts.event: United States tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel rise to 50%
catalysts.rationale: A dated, pre-announced escalation just beyond the strategic window that extends the quote leg's tariff exposure well past the current 5.2% of bilateral exports and strikes the auto sector directly. Because Section 338 carries no expiry, it persists until a presidential proclamation removes it. It is the reason Factor 7 is scored more confidently strategically than tactically and the reason the quote leg's tail is structurally fatter than the base leg's.

Implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote: AUD/CAD has no listed option, so the surface is derived from the variance identity using a realised correlation of 0.4963 in place of an unobservable implied one, understating by a documented median 14.4% across seventeen pairs. The 6.611% figure at 94.7 days is treated as a floor; a plausible true 3M ATM is 7.0–7.6%. There are no risk reversals, butterflies or vol-of-vol quotable for this cross at any tenor.

Realised volatility discrepancy: the price payload records 60-day realised volatility of 5.14%; the base dossier's cache carries 5.58% for the same cross. The payload governs per the framework's data-source rules; the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.318 on the estimated implied basis, 0.376 on the dossier's realised basis and 0.409 on the payload's — a cache-vintage difference rather than an analytical disagreement.

Forward points are derived, not quoted: outrights are computed from the CME calendar-spread funding premium of −231.1bp annualised (6A/6C, 13.6 to 48.6 days, observed 2026-08-31), applied on an actual/365 basis to spot and extrapolated linearly beyond the observation window. This premium equals the interest differential plus cross-currency basis and is not the policy differential. Derived outrights are accurate to roughly one to two pips at one month and three to five at six months.

Yield spreads are on a monthly basis: the bilateral 10-year differential of +141.1bp is computed from AUD 4.831% and CAD 3.42%, both the monthly series as of 2026-06-01, and is never quoted as a live spread.

Resistance zone shortfall handled by supplementation and disclosure: because zero resistance zones met the two-touch threshold, the resistance list is assembled from the payload's own 52-week extremes, round numbers, and one externally identified supply band (0.9950–1.0000), labelled as supplements rather than computed zones. Support zones are quoted verbatim from the payload, ranked by touch count, with distances to zone midpoints.

Valuation methodology: no PPP series exists for this cross, so the valuation read is a relative BIS REER gap on June 2026 observations roughly 63 days before the valuation date and marginally outside the 60-day strategic freshness window. This measures relative real misalignment, not fair value; the implied 0.82 level from full gap closure is explicitly not a forecast.

Bilateral trade taken from the injected block, not re-estimated: IMF DOTS 2024 figures (AU exports to Canada US$2.1bn, imports US$2.7bn, net −US$0.6bn) are used directly in Factor 5. A separate government source reports 2025 bilateral goods trade at C$7.8bn and services at C$4.6bn with differing currency/year bases, disclosed rather than reconciled. FDI stocks are used as bilateral context only and not netted into Factor 5's terms-of-trade calculation.

The ABS national-accounts basis is preferred; direction is common to both but magnitude is flagged as unresolved.

Consensus reported as located, not manufactured: no named investment bank publishes an AUD/CAD forecast that could be sourced. The Exchange Rates UK multi-provider aggregate is labelled as an aggregate with disclosed methodology; retail extrapolation sites are excluded on principle as scripts on ad-supported pages, though one is mentioned for completeness because it leans the opposite way. The derived cross of named-bank AUD/USD and USD/CAD legs is labelled as derived.
